title: Standard method for microCT-based additive manufacturing quality control 2: density measurement
author: Anton Du Plessis
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.sbvean6

steps.title: Prepare Sample and Equipment
steps.instruction: Prepare a 10 x 10 x 10 mm cube coupon sample and a scale with accuracy to 3 digits.

substeps.instruction: Load the sample in foam at an angle to ensure no edge artifacts are present.

steps.title: Perform MicroCT Scan
steps.instruction: Scan the sample using a laboratory microCT system with a 15 µm voxel size and the following parameters:

substeps.instruction: Set voltage to 200 kV and current to 70 uA.
Set image acquisition to 500 ms per image.
Perform a full 360 degree rotation with 2400 step positions.
Discard the first image at each step position and average the two subsequent images.

steps.title: Reconstruct Scan Data
steps.instruction: Reconstruct the images using a strong beam hardening correction factor without any image de-noising.

steps.title: Segment Sample Volume
steps.instruction: Analyze the data in Volume Graphics VGStudioMax 3.1 to determine the total object volume, including internal pores but excluding exterior air.

substeps.instruction: Create a region of interest (ROI) from this surface.
Modify the ROI using an opening/closing function with a value of +3 to close small surface pores.
Use a region growing tool with high tolerance on the air outside the part, selecting the option to 'avoid other visible ROIs'.
If noise particles (e.g., loose powder) are present outside the part, apply an opening/closing function (+3) to this exterior region to remove them.
Invert the exterior-air selection to select the entire part including internal voids.
Apply a new advanced surface determination function using this ROI selection as a starting contour for sub-voxel precision on the surface location.

steps.title: Calculate Average Density
steps.instruction: Determine the accurate total volume of the part from the properties tab of the final object and combine this with the part mass measured by the scale to calculate the average density.
